We introduce global dynamical scaling laws for three-state quantum transitions, where a system evolves from an initial steady state into a final topologically distinct stationary regime separated by a critical sub-phase. Using a unified method based on time-energy uncertainty and a general quantum classification, these principles are demonstrated using a model of free-quantum spreading with obstacles. The derived scaling rules apply to a broad range of quantum critical phenomena within dynamical evolution.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) have recently achieved state-of-the-art results in various computer vision tasks, surpassing CNN architectures. Despite this success, ViTs often struggle with interpretability, as their internal decision-making processes remain obscure. To address this gap, this study investigates the nature of visual features (traits) within self-supervised Vision Transformers across multiple layer depths. By employing an input-output visualization technique, we reveal that early layers encode high-frequency local details, whereas subsequent layers capture increasingly abstract characteristics such as specific object parts and entire categories. Furthermore, we examine the relationships between ViT traits and those developed by CNNs through both clustering and dimensionality reduction methods. Our findings suggest that while self-supervised ViTs develop distinct features, there is substantial alignment with CNN representations at the level of object and component classification. Ultimately, these insights provide deeper knowledge of Vision Transformers, facilitating enhanced interpretability and offering a foundation for future performance improvements.

We investigate an idealized dissipative cosmological model incorporating a single fluid representing both dark matter and dark energy. The evolution equations, governed by the parameters $w_{0}$ and $w_{1}$, are solved numerically. A stability analysis of the resulting solutions is performed. Specifically, we examine the dissipative $\Lambda$CDM scenario ($w_{0}=-1, w_{1}= 0$) and compare our findings with observations from the Planck 2018 dataset. The results demonstrate that our model is observationally viable and distinctively differs from its non-dissipative counterpart.

We provide a direct demonstration of the ill-posedness of the incompressible Euler equations within certain critical Sobolev spaces ($\dot{H}^{s}\otimes\dot{H}^{s}$ with $s\leq 1$) and critical Besov spaces ($\dot{B}^{1}_{\infty}\otimes\dot{B}^{1}_{\infty}$). Our approach relies on a universal finite-dimensional invariant manifold for the Euler equations established by Kato and Témam, combined with an independent result by Kato and Enright regarding the instability of the zero solution in a specific regime ($s>1$ but close to 1). This methodology also allows us to prove that the instability result by finite-time blow-up for the 3D quasi-geostrophic equation in the critical case ($Q_{crit}$) applies directly to the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations.

Although recent advancements in image generation models have produced remarkable results, researchers are increasingly seeking more precise image synthesis and editing capabilities. This study introduces Steady Creator (DCT-50), a framework designed to control image editing within the latent space of the image diffusion model. By leveraging a "Steady Point" within latent space that maintains structural consistency across conditions, our method enables the directed alteration of specific attributes, such as changing the hue in an image through "staying points." This approach allows control over properties like hair color without unintentionally modifying other structural elements. You can access our pre-trained DCT-50 model at: https://github.com/yzhao062/steady_creator.

We introduce a deep neural network framework designed for reversible image Steganography, utilizing Bayesian Neural Networks to guarantee exact pixel-wise recoverability. By employing the Monte Carlo Dropout technique, we determine model uncertainties to train a loss function that optimizes the balance between high embedding capacity and guaranteeing complete pixel recoverability. This research also covers the adaptation of the model across high and low resolution domains, as well as color/grayscale conversions, further detailing how the method performs under these specific conditions.

We investigate the implications of a hypothetical, yet experimentally constrained, $J/\psi$ decay into invisible particles. This constraint establishes an upper limit on the ratio $\Gamma/\gamma \lesssim 10^{-27}$, where the term represents transitions to photons. This bound enables us to connect such a limit to the mass scale of neutrinos and dark energy within the framework of effective field theories, specifically assuming a single dimensionless coupling governs all sectors. Under this assumption, the bound yields a heavy mediator mass exceeding 10^10^7 Gev. Furthermore, it suggests the existence of extremely suppressed operators that could account for both light neutrino masses and the observed value of dark energy density.

This study introduces new observational evidence supporting the coexistence of a two-part distribution in solar magnetic luminous spots. Derived from a dataset of high-resolution magnetograms collected by SDO/MDI, the research reveals that large solar magnetic spots follow a two-part distribution characterized by dual exponential decay rates, whereas small solar magnetic spots are best described by a single-exponential distribution.

This study examines the structure and nature of dynamic identification models through an anthropocentric lens, utilizing a collection of films crafted by humans as a case dataset. Since these films represent dynamic systems, their system identification models inherently reflect the attributes of human-centric id models. We argue that these films are not merely a random assortment; rather, the systems they depict are governed by laws of nature, suggesting that the resulting models mirror the theoretical anthropocentric framework. The research begins by outlining theories regarding how humans construct identification models for dynamic systems, then proceeds to analyze and compare these theoretical predictions with the actual models derived from the films.

We conclude that monodirectional dark matter cannot be monopole-like, as such monopoles would cause a significant depletion of the cosmic microwave background's blackbody spectrum. Additionally, we propose an alternative: a spin-1/2 monopole with an extremely low mass (around 10^-32 to 10^-34 eV) acting as a self-conjugate particle. This particle interacts with its environment through two mechanisms: a weak, long-range force due to its monopole nature, causing spin precession in ambient magnetic fields, and a short-range interaction allowing it to act as its own antiparticle. This theoretical model explains why no dark matter direct detection experiments have succeeded so far. Furthermore, we show that this mini-magnetic monopole can accumulate within the Milky Way's central region, forming a halo with a peak density reaching approximately 10^-6 times the standard local dark matter density. We calculate that this accumulation is sufficient to sustain the galaxy's magnetic field over billions of years by providing continuous energy to counteract Ohmic dissipation.

Accurately forecasting climate change is vital for safeguarding ecological stability and ensuring food and water security. However, existing methods often fail to fully exploit the intricate spatiotemporal relationships within climate datasets. This study introduces TSWT, a novel network designed for predicting spatiotemporal variables by integrating self-attention over patches, two-dimensional temporal self-attention, and a two-way linear embedding strategy. Specifically, TSWT partitions the input data into windowed grids, applying self-attention mechanisms to the resulting patches to efficiently capture local spatial dependencies. It further enhances the model with 2-D temporal self-attention to detect correlations across time steps within each grid, effectively generalizing the problem. This mechanism allows the network to understand long-range temporal dynamics while maintaining sensitivity to precise timing. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that TSWT significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in forecasting efficiency.

We analyze scenarios involving either two scalar pairs alongside their parities, or three pairs alongside their parities, maintaining invariance under the discrete symmetry group D6 for the respective matter sectors. We investigate scenarios with broken or unbroken symmetry groups, exploring mass spectrum possibilities, production mechanisms at the Large Hadron Collider, and decay channels. Our results demonstrate that this architecture offers two viable dark matter candidates with distinct mass ranges, contingent on specific model parameters. Furthermore, this framework establishes two distinct three-Higgs-Doublet Models (HDM3) distinguished by dark matter interactions, specifically the even-even and odd-even types based on how fields transform under the symmetry group. Our study reveals that these models support two shadow matter candidates with different mass scales, governed by specific coupling constants and potential energy parameters within the system symmetry. We explore how these frameworks define unique HDM3 structures through specific dark matter interaction patterns, specifically the even-even and odd-even interaction types determined by specific parity assignments under discrete symmetry groups. In this study, we formulate a mathematical model to simulate ion transport within neurons, accounting for ion channel regulation and congestion effects. Our objective function aims to stabilize neuronal ion levels by minimizing deviations from target concentrations, subject to PDEs representing ions' congested dynamics governed by the Navier-Stege equations with Squire flow and Fick's second law of diffusion. To address this PDE-constrained optimization challenge, we derive the objective function's gradient using an adjoint state technique and implement our approach using the IPOPS solver available in the CasADi framework. Validation of the proposed model and optimization framework is performed using two standard neuronal morphologies: the simplified ball-and-stick structure and detailed experimental data for a CA3 hippocampal pyramidal neuron.

Despite the widespread adoption of blockchain technology, its benefits remain underappreciated by the banking sector due to persistent challenges such as scalability, privacy, and interoperability. To address these gaps, we introduce NeMo, a novel concept derived from merging two complementary sub-blockchains, each tailored to resolve specific pairs of challenges. By network motif analysis, we identify an optimal topological structure for network integration that effectively mitigates these issues while maximizing blockchain advantages. To validate our approach, we construct and evaluate a prototype integrating NeMo into a design featuring the IBS and IBTK consensus mechanisms. Our findings demonstrate that this proposed solution offers a viable path to fully realizing the blockchain solution for banking challenges.

We have performed 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations to examine the star's emissions as it is consumed by a supermassive black hole, a process that can mimic the signatures of the tidal disruption event (TDE) where a star is devoured. The scenario involves a star reaching the point of direct disruption at the black hole's horizon, an event that results in the immediate accretion of the star's material. The event horizon acts as an anchor for the magnetic field lines, which, combined with the infalling material, generate strong magnetic fields within the black hole's accretion flow. These fields drive powerful jets, which are responsible for the majority of the radiated energy. The simulations reveal that the jets are highly collimated and originate from the innermost regions of the system, while the accretion disk forms further out. The event horizon's role in twisting magnetic field lines is the mechanism that launches and shapes these energetic jets.

This paper examines the hadronic currents governing semilectonic $\tau$-decays into three-body final states consisting of a lepton and two hadrons. For three specific reaction channels, explicit representations of the hadronic matrix elements are provided in terms of eight shape factors. These representation schemes are derived by employing the most general set of Lorentz structures, utilizing four-momenta of the outgoing hadrons, alongside the standard representation based on the momentum transfer between the initial and final baryonic states. The study further explores the physical implications regarding form factor normalizations, form factor relationships, and constraints on form factor behavior near zero momentum transfer. Finally, constraints imposed by isospin and G-parity symmetries are analyzed.

The paper's focus lies in the metric known as Tversky distance, which generalizes the concept of the Jaccard distance. We demonstrate that the Tversky distance offers a metric space structure for all non-negative values except exactly one specific real number. By utilizing this unique excluded value, we pinpoint a corresponding value that acts as a parallel to the normalized information distance distance. We also explore the implications of this relationship within T-space and suggest a potential application in information theory.

Deblurring deformed images containing humans or scenes is a difficult task due to ambiguous reconstruction possibilities. To address this, we introduce a new approach for deblurring distorted images of people or settings by utilizing a pseudo-blur conditional generative adversarial network (pCGAN). Our method creates deblurred content that is conditionally aligned with the underlying 3D structure of the original image. This alignment helps the network generate a more singular, structurally coherent latent representation, effectively resolving ambiguity. The proposed deep learning-based era-of-information scheduling (DL-EIS) algorithm determines RB allocation and power strategies within an acceptable timeframe with guaranteed convergence. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the complexity of the proposed DSD scheme is significantly lower than that of conventional methods, while DL-EIS substantially improves D2D sum rates compared to existing orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA)-based scheduling approaches.

This paper presents an analysis of the 3D compressible Euler equations featuring haptically invariant initial data. We establish the local existence of solutions alongside helicity maintenance, a result achievable through a simplified definition of the pressure function $p(\rho)$—specifically as $\rho\gamma(\log\rho + 1 + p_0)$. This specific form of the pressure law streamlines calculations compared to standard assumptions like $p(\rho) = \rho^\gamma$. Additionally, our findings extend beyond previous studies by not mandating bounds on the $L^\infty$ norm for the gradient of density, $\nabla\log\rho$. However, it is important to note that the derived local existence interval is not optimal.

This study employs post-Newtonian theory to investigate how small eccentricities dissipate in compact binary systems over long durations. We derive an analytical expression for the asymptotic eccentricity residual ($e_{\rm res}$) derived from the balance between eccentricity growth due to adiabatic changes in an orbit's timescale of relaxation and its decay due to gravitational-wave (GW) emission. Comparisons with numerical integrations of GW-driven binaries confirm that this formula accurately captures the long-term evolution of eccentricity down to $e\sim10^{-3}$. For an observed $e_{\rm res}\sim10^{-3}$ at the gravitational-wave detection threshold, we derive constraints on the source population: an inclination-averaged asymptotic eccentricity ($e_{\rm i}$) of $\gtrsim0.1$ is required for sources with frequencies ($f_{\rm i}$) $\lesssim0.03$ times the GW inspiral frequency at merger. These limits apply to both stellar-mass mergers detected by LIGO/Virgo and supermassive black hole coalescences observed by LISA.

The Advanced Photon Source Upgrade Project (APS-U) at Argonne National Laboratory is designed to deliver the world's most advanced capabilities for high-power synchrotron radiation research. This initiative involves a major upgrade of the existing APS facility, transforming it into a third-generation light source with dual rings operating at third-harmonic resonance. This configuration aims to achieve peak stored beam energies of up to 500 kJ in both the ultraviolet and visible light frequencies. This paper details the design and performance characteristics of the APS High-Luminosity Coherent X-ray Upgrade (AXRE), a $10^9$-times amplification system based on the existing undulator infrastructure. The primary objective of AXRE is to generate fully coherent beams with up to 500 kW peak power for advanced applications. This concept relies on integrating existing high-gain optical amplifiers with a compact, table-top Free-Electron Laser (FEL) oscillator. The proposed FEL oscillator is engineered for compactness, occupying a small area while maintaining high efficiency and stability. This design enables precise control over coherent beam parameters—including energy, pulse length, and stability—and allows for the generation of two independently controllable, ultra-short pulse trains.

Accurately tracking incident progression within networks is crucial for maintaining service quality and ensuring network reliability. Although tracking incidents on static networks is well-established, the scenario involving dynamic networks remains under-researched. This paper introduces a novel method for incident detection on dynamic networks by introducing a new dynamic k-means clustering algorithm that accounts for link evolution. By representing each detection point as a snapshot and applying this modified clustering, we construct a temporal evolution graph to visualize incident progression. This approach is grounded in the assumption that dynamically formed clusters represent near-optimal groupings, preserving essential network topological features. The validity of this assumption was confirmed through both real-world experiments and mathematical proofs. Results from testing on various dynamic networks demonstrated that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing standard k-means variants across multiple metrics, including time complexity, clustering error rates, and silhouette scores.

Investigating interfaces within a high-density medium subject to shocks, this study examines the dynamics of a shock wave traveling through a perfect gas with density $\rho_0$ and polytropic exponent $\gamma$, where $\rho_0$ varies spatially according to a power law of density ratio $\eta$. The analysis derives the conditions for both the prevention and elimination of intermediate shocks by analyzing an integral representing the geometric area enclosed by the intersection of shock and sound curves on a $(p, u)$ diagram. It is demonstrated that when the medium's density change exponent $\eta$ is greater than $-\gamma$, a necessary condition for intermediate shock formation is $\eta > -\gamma$; this criterion is subsequently verified against established literature.

Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly shaping critical real-world decisions across domains such as healthcare and justice, creating an urgent need for transparency regarding how these systems operate. Consequently, the core objective of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is to make ML and AI understandable to humans. While current XAI research predominantly targets technical aspects—such as model explainability and researcher understanding—there remains a significant gap in exploring the human side, specifically the understandability of XEXAI from the perspective of its end-users. This study addresses that deficiency by applying requirements engineering practices to bridge the divide. We present a methodology that enables stakeholders to collaboratively define, categorize, and prioritize the kinds of explanations necessary for targeted user groups. Furthermore, we introduce a flexible framework adaptable to various priority strategies and document our industry experience implementing this approach.

We present **UniToPatho**, a novel dataset of histopathological images of colorectal polyps, featuring extensive annotations for classification and adenoma grading. The collection comprises 1,000 representative low-magnification images (×40) and 1,000 representative high-magnification images (×400) that address the scarcity found in current resources. Each image is tagged with:
*   **Colorectal Polyp Classification:** Hyperplastic, Adenomatous, or Serrated.
*   **Adenoma Grading:** Mild, Moderate, or Severe.
*   **Segmentation Masks:** Precise outlines for the entire polyp and specific regions for gland structures.
*   **Textual Descriptions:** Detailed narrative reports written by expert pathologists.
*   **Imaging Data:** Associated radiology reports providing the endoscopic context for each slide.

To ensure maximum utility, our goal was to create a resource capable of supporting state-of-the-art research in computer-aided diagnosis for removing adenomas from images and generating accurate, high-quality pathology reports via automated generation techniques.

This research investigates data leakage within the framework of zero-error source encoding, a model where encoders and decoders operate under constraints that forbid ambiguous reconstructions. We establish connections between the mutual information quantifying the total data leakage and various graph theoretical metrics of the underlying confusion graphs, specifically leveraging parameters such as the size, vertex cover, and clique number. Our analysis also introduces the leakage-specific graph, termed a coautoencoding graph, to which we prove that its vertex cover size constitutes a tight upper bound on mutual information leakage. Furthermore, we present network architectures that achieve this bound, effectively making it equal to the derived bound through three distinct classes of networks: random graphs, complete bipartite graphs, and certain symmetric autoencoding networks.

Deep generative models have proven highly effective for synthesizing realistic high-resolution (HR) images from low-resolution (LR) inputs, yet they frequently fail to capture complex, data-driven mapping functions during super-resolution tasks. This study introduces MrSARP, a hierarchical deep generative framework designed to enhance complex mapping modeling by integrating multi-reference multi-anchor representations. The model employs a dual-anchor mechanism: one derived directly from the input LR image and another sourced from a pre-trained anchor image library to create a hybrid representation. Leveraging the inherent characteristics of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, which maintains consistency across large areas, we construct a database of standard reference images. Consequently, this approach yields two distinct maps: a single global transformation and multiple localized, spatially constrained transformations. To ensure SAR-specific image synthesis, a comprehensive pre-computation of feature correlation matrices (ECMs) serves as the foundation for both mapping strategies. Furthermore, a multi-objective loss function, combining super-resolution fidelity with SAR image consistency, optimizes the entire architecture. Extensive experiments on SAR datasets demonstrate that MrSARP significantly outperforms both traditional methods and existing deep learning algorithms in terms of sharpness, detail, and overall structural accuracy.

Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (QAOAs) represent a hybrid quantum-classical framework designed for solving combinatorial optimization challenges. While effective, QAOA encounters the "barren plateau" issue as problem dimensions expand, causing quantum gradient amplitudes to exponentially diminish and thereby impairing classical optimizers' ability to navigate the cost function landscape efficiently. This paper proposes a Bayesian enhancement for QAOA to mitigate such inefficiencies. By employing Bayesian inference to refine the search for optimal parameters, our method reduces the resource requirements for achieving target precision. Furthermore, we demonstrate enhanced convergence for the hybrid system specifically under the "barren plateau" scenario through theoretical analysis.

This paper outlines an approach to identify the common area defined by any set of ellipses. It introduces an algorithm capable of locating ellipse intersections using an orientation-sensitive method, with a time complexity of $O(N^3)$ for $N$ ellipses. The resulting decomposition expresses the common area as a union of convex regions, each being either empty, a single ellipse, or a two-ellipse intersection. Each such region is described through a constant number ($O(1)$) of geometric elements, including portions of at most two full ellipses bounded by specific intersection points, or an attached segment of at least one closed ellipse defined by at least one such point.

This framework operates by applying an adaptive factor of $q$ to scale down gradients based on the specific characteristics of the function landscape at any given point. The value of this gradient scaler is not fixed; it is learned online and adjusts dynamically throughout training. We investigate an extended Hubbard model on a triangular lattice featuring nearest-neighbor hopping and second-nearest-neighbor Coulomb repulsion ($J$), employing density matrix renormalization group techniques on cylinder geometries. Our findings indicate that at low temperatures, the system supports magnetic oscillations that persist regardless of the values of interaction ($U$) or ($J$). We propose that these long-range correlations stem from an emergent SU(2) symmetry present in the effective Hamiltonian, similar to the kagome case, allowing us to map the physics onto a Heisenberg model with alternating ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic bonds. Additionally, we examine the implications of emergent SU(2) symmetry regarding the "order-by-disorder" phenomenon, aligning our results with prior quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, we outline a framework to elucidate the diverse ground-state behaviors, including valence-bond solids, antiferromagnets, and potentially quantum spin liquids.

Vertebrae localization and recognition are essential for spinal analysis and CT-based diagnostics. This paper introduces a new approach to automate this process using single axial CT slices. Drawing on anatomical knowledge, we constrain a U-Net neural network to extract only the vertebrae and their surrounding boundary, discarding other organs to enhance focus. To further leverage anatomy, we apply a guided curve fitting technique that realigns the images around the vertebrae. This realignment ensures a consistent layout across slices, which enhances the model's ability to learn effective features for identification. Experiments demonstrate that this proposed framework surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods in detecting and recognizing vertebrae.

In stochastic processes, the trajectory of a particle can be modeled as a trace, and its statistical attributes can be analyzed using the framework of stochastic thermodynamics. This approach allows us to derive random currents that correspond to standard physical currents but possess inherent statistical fluctuations. Our investigation focuses on the asymptotic statistical distributions of these random variables as the duration tends toward infinity. We demonstrate that the distribution's dependence on the specific dynamical rules is merely a multiplicative factor and prove that, for all stochastic systems, a single universal distribution exists for time-reversible systems. This finding establishes the gauge invariance of asymptotic distributions within the field, showing that the standard dynamical laws of stochastic stochastic thermodynamics stem from this property. The study extends to varying speeds and includes an exploration of the connections between these varying speeds and thermodynamic duality.

We investigate the behavior of relative quantum homology for manifolds with boundary when subjected to rational functions. As a specific application, we establish the established long exact sequence in relative quantum cohomology for tori.

When two piezoelectric materials are placed in close proximity, stress generated by a acoustic wave in the first can trigger a corresponding wave in the second. This study examines the interaction of such waves in two quartz crystals separated by half a wavelength, focusing on cases where the boundary conditions are either free or rigid. The results demonstrate that if a wave initiates in the first quartz crystal, it transmits entirely into the second. This phenomenon, which represents the extreme case of partial coupling, arises because mechanical and electrical energies within the first crystal couple with those in the second through mechanical stress, while wave reflections within each quartz crystal prevent total energy dissipation.

Pursuing new physical mechanisms to control quantum many-body systems is a central objective in contemporary research. Recently, it was demonstrated that integrating optical microcavities with two-dimensional materials enables access to diverse phenomena, including persistent currents, entanglement, and correlation distributions. This advancing field is known as "semiconductor optics." In this paper, we introduce and explore another direction by merging non-Abelian gauge fields with fluid dynamics within large collections of exciton-polaritons. Our proposed framework involves applying a stochastic phase to the material wavefunction through a moving optical trap, a strategy that generates gauge forces and yields Galilean-invariant dynamics reminiscent of reservoir optics. We examine the resulting phase space structures and demonstrate that the generated gauge forces can produce striking effects, such as modifying two-dimensional correlation patterns and creating asymmetries in energy distributions.

The newly identified ultra-short-period binary system, K2-22 b, comprises a transiting hot Jupiter orbiting a K2 dwarf star. Our recent observations utilizing the Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Large Binocular Telescope reveal that light curves at 3.8 micrometers are significantly deeper than those obtained in the optical range. This discrepancy strongly indicates the presence of a massive, optically thick circumplanetary dust cloud. Spectral fitting suggests this dust cloud contains large grains exceeding 3.8 micrometers in size. Additionally, spectral features observed from system to Earth imply an optically thin gas envelope surrounding the dust, indicative of high-velocity outflows. These atmospheric escape mechanisms result in a mass loss rate of approximately $10^{-5}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr, which is orders of magnitude higher than typical values. Consequently, these clouds likely play a critical role in shaping the current orbit and future evolution of the planet.

This paper introduces Daany, a .NET-based data analysis framework. It offers a suite of tools for dataset creation, manipulation, and statistical analysis, featuring significant similarities to Python's Pand library and the Anaconda distribution. This document provides an overview of the framework's core architecture and implementation details of its various components.

This paper examines the opposing views on the role of mathematics in the natural sciences during the Scientific Renaissance, highlighting the distinction made by figures like Galileo between two approaches: one where mathematics serves as a descriptive aid within qualitative philosophical frameworks, versus a second that integrates it seamlessly into scientific reasoning. The discussion centers on the debate between these positions, utilizing the concepts advanced by Wilhelm Ostwald and Paul Forman, as well as the specific argument put forward by Thomas Aquinas, to explore how each approach influenced science in the Renaissance period.

Saha's equation, which is widely used in cosmology, is frequently criticized for its neglect of ion recombination, leading many to prefer the more rigorous two-level kinetic framework. However, this study demonstrates that the Saha model, despite its flaws, can still describe ionization dynamics accurately if Saha's original formulation is extended to incorporate a Saha-Chandrasekhar two-equilibrium model. By chandrasekhar, we refer to a set of two equations that simultaneously address ionization and recombination to enable a accurate representation of these processes. By utilizing this extension, we re-evaluated ionization in the early Universe and discovered that non-linearities in Saha's law can generate non-Gaussian signatures in the primordial power spectrum. Specifically, the amplitude and shape of these non-Gaussianities are sensitive to ionization history; thus, CMB observations of the three-point correlation function could potentially be used to refine our knowledge of ionization during the early cosmos.

This study employs a hybrid model where magnetic field lines are treated as fluid elements with finite thickness, allowing for the integration of fluid equations to characterize magnetic reconnection. Applied to magnetic islands in the reversed field pinch configuration, this approach enables the direct computation of merging dynamics. By juxtapacing simulations using pure magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) with those incorporating the novel hybrid technique, we examine both small-scale merging and large-scale evolution. Results indicate that while the hybrid method accurately reproduces the reconnection rate consistent with MHD predictions, it yields different behaviors regarding island coalescence. Specifically, three distinct merging protocols are identified as the size of merging islands varies relative to field line thickness. Furthermore, because this method explicitly models kinetic effects, it successfully captures ion-acoustic waves generated during the reconnection process.

This study introduces Amanuensis, an advanced code-suggestion tool designed to integrate seamlessly within the primary development workflows of current programmers. Evaluated against leading industrial alternatives in a challenging, real-world coding context, results demonstrate that Amanuensis significantly boosts programming productivity. Furthermore, by analyzing a decade of programming education literature, we explore how these productivity gains can seep into broader societal impacts, specifically aiding the training of future software developers.
